# In Praise of the Unnoticed

Try this. Put down your phone and watch the light on the wall. Not the sun, not the window, not the clock. Just the light—the way it rests on the plaster, the slight trembling of its edge, the dust that hangs in its beam like a slow constellation. Do that for one minute. It will feel like an indulgence, then like an embarrassment, and finally, if you last long enough, like a revelation. The light moves. It moves? The earth moves, and the light is the messenger of that movement. It is the visible proof of spin, though we usually do not look long enough to see it.

I began to pay attention to such things by accident. I was waiting for something—a phone call, a test result, a letter that never arrived—and the waiting made ordinary surfaces unbearable and then unbearably interesting. The crack in the ceiling above my bed became a geography. The stain on the bookshelf became a Rorschach. The slow crawl of a spider across the baseboard became a narrative, complete with obstacles and a triumphant conclusion, the conclusion being that the spider disappeared into a crack and I did not see it die. This is what waiting does: it strips the world of its usefulness and leaves it as pure spectacle. It is the cheapest form of travel.

Attention is the only currency that cannot be inflated. There is always enough of it, yet we spend it as if it were worthless. We give it to screens that have been designed, by very intelligent people, to seize it and sell it. We give it to anxiety about the future and guilt about the past. We give it to the next thing before the present thing has even arrived. And then we wonder why time feels thin, why we cannot remember Tuesday, why the years slip by like water through a sieve. The paradox is that time does not slip by quickly; we slip by time quickly. To slow down, all we have to do is notice.

This is not a new idea. Every contemplative tradition says something like it. But I am not a mystic, and I don't intend to become one. I am just a person who has discovered that a dirty window, in the right light, can be as beautiful as a cathedral. There is a particular moment in late autumn, around four in the afternoon, when the sun comes through the west-facing window of my kitchen and strikes the flyspecked glass of the cabinet. The marks become a star chart. The pale yellow light reveals the film of grease left by years of cooking, the fingerprints of every meal I have ever made in that room. It is not clean, and that is the point. A spotless kitchen has no history. A clean window is just a hole. The dirty window is a text, written by time, illuminated by light.

I want to write a field guide to such texts. Not to grand landscapes, not to the Grand Canyon or the northern lights or the perfect beach at sunset—the postcard places where everyone already knows to look. I want to write about the overlooked. The architecture of a puddle. The voice of a radiator in December. The particular geometry of a grocery store parking lot at twilight. The way a plastic bag, caught in a bush, can look like a strange flower. The sound of your own breathing when you finally stop to listen to it. These are not escapes from the world. They are the world, if the world is large enough to include the insignificant.

When I was a child, my grandparents had a garden. It was not a beautiful garden. It was a working garden, a vegetable garden, full of weeds and stubborn soil and the skeletal remains of tomato cages. My grandfather would come in from it at dusk, his hands stained green, his shirt stuck to his back. He would set a basket of tomatoes on the counter and say, “Taste one.” I did. It was warm from the sun, still dusty, and it tasted like nothing I have since encountered—not because tomatoes have changed, but because I have changed. The tomato was a verb. It was the entire month of August compressed into a single fragrant globe.

I could not have said that then. I would have said, “It’s good,” and run off to do something else. But the memory stayed, and it has become one of my most durable possessions. I carry it around like a coin in my pocket. Sometimes I take it out and examine it: the green smell of the vines, the white-painted farmhouse behind me, the sound of my grandmother singing along to a radio in a language I didn’t understand. Why this moment and not a hundred others? I have asked myself this question for years. There is no answer. Memory is not a filing system. It is an ocean, and certain moments bob to the surface while others sink without a trace.

Proust had his madeleine. Marcel had his little cake, and I have my tasteless supermarket tomatoes, which are the exact opposite of the thing they recall. The madeleine is not a madeleine. It is any object that opens the door. For some people it is a song, a particular song from a particular summer, and for a second they are sixteen again, standing in a parking lot with the windows down. For others it is a smell: sunscreen, chlorine, rain on hot asphalt. These are not memories in the usual sense. They are resurrections. The past is not behind us. It is folded into the present, waiting for a cue.

We spend so much of our lives trying to escape the present—through memory, through anticipation, through the tiny anesthesia of the scroll—that we forget the present is the only place where the past can leak through. A friend of mine once said that nostalgia is not a longing for a time; it is a longing for a body. The body we had then. The knees that could kneel without pain, the eyes that did not need glasses, the skin that did not know the weight of years. The garden exists because my child-body existed in it. The tomato tastes the way it does because my mouth was new. Grief and wonder are the same organ, the sense that can touch the past.

And yet, I do not want to live in memory. The trick is to let memory dim the present just enough to give it depth, like a shadow in a painting. When I walk through the city today, I am walking through two cities: the one that is here and the one that used to be here. The drugstore where I bought my first concert ticket is now a laundromat. The movie theater has been torn down, and the parking lot has been filled with a sleek apartment building with a sign that says “LUXURY LIVING.” The maple tree I used to climb is gone, but the shape of its absence is still visible in the skyline. A tree can die, but the negative space it leaves behind is a kind of monument.

The same is true for people. On the street I sometimes see a man who looks exactly like my father did when I was ten—same jacket, same way of holding his shoulders—and for a split second, hope surges: he is alive, he is young, he is walking toward me. Then the man turns, and it is not him, and the hope collapses into something like vertigo. But I do not want to stop having these moments. They are the proof that the past is not finished. They are the proof that love leaves an imprint, the way a body leaves a warm spot in a chair.

I am a writer, which means I spend a large part of my life failing to describe things. This is not a confession; it is a job description. The sunset cannot be captured. The face of a sleeping child cannot be captured. The exact weight of a particular silence, in a particular room, with a particular person, cannot be captured. And yet we keep trying. Why? Because the attempt to capture something is itself a way of paying attention. It is a way of asking the world to stay still long enough for us to love it.

Writing is an act of attention performed in public. A good description is not a photograph; it is a map. The map, as every cartographer knows, is not the territory. But a good map can teach you to see the territory for yourself. It can point to a hill and say, “Look, there is a hill,” and when you look, you see the hill, and you also see something the map did not include—a bird, a shadow, a wind that moves the grass. The map’s grammar is not the world’s grammar, but it can rhyme with it.

I have a notebook full of failed descriptions. It is my favorite possession. I open it and read: “The fog came in like a cat that does not want to be petted.” That is a good simile, but it is also a lie. The fog has no intention. It is only fog. The simile is a map of my feeling, not of the fog. Another entry: “The station clock is permanently ten minutes fast, and the green light above the platform buzzes like a trapped fly.” This is almost a description, but it omits the most important thing: the smell of diesel and rain, the sound of a woman’s heels receding on the platform, the fact that I was late and did not care. Too much to include. The writer must choose, and every choice is a loss.

But sometimes, rarely, a description fails so beautifully that it creates a new organ of perception. I read a poem about a river and, for a week, I cannot look at a river without hearing the poet’s sound. I read a novel about a city and, for a month, the city is thicker. The novel has added a ghost floor to every building, a secret passage to every street. This is not magic. It is simply the power of one person’s attention, transmitted through black marks on a page, to teach another person how to look. It is the same power that makes a parent say to a child, “See the moon?” and the child, looking up, sees the moon for the first time even though it has been there every night. We do not see the world. We see what we have been taught to see. Attention is learned. Wonder is a skill.

Of course, attention is contested territory. I do not need to describe the screen; you are reading this on one. It is the world’s most effective attention trap, and I am using it while denouncing it. That is the peculiar position of anyone who writes about distraction: you cannot escape the medium you address. But I can at least tell the truth about my own experience. When I am scrolling, I am not paying attention. I am being taken for a ride. My eyes move across a river of opinions, advertisements, photographs, outrage, all of it engineered to produce a micro-response—a jab of anger, a pinch of envy, a brief hollow amusement. Each response resets the clock. The algorithm dangles the next bait. It is as if someone had invented a machine for the express purpose of converting my life into a series of ten-second glances, and then paid me no wages.

The strange thing is that I know this. We all know this. And yet the compulsion persists. The phone is not a tool; it is a companion, a pet, an appendage. I have caught myself stroking its screen as if it were a cat. I have reached for it in the middle of a conversation with a friend, and then realized what I was doing, and then realized that I was reaching for it again to escape the shame of having reached for it. The only way out is not through willpower, which is finite and easily exhausted. It is through the reclamation of boredom. We have forgotten how to be bored. We treat boredom as an emergency, as a symptom to be suppressed. But boredom is the antechamber of attention. It is the empty room where wonder can enter.

Some of my most profound experiences have occurred while doing apparently nothing. Waiting for bread to rise. Staring out the window of a train. Lying in bed and watching the shadows of leaves move on the ceiling. In these moments, I have solved problems I did not know I had, remembered people I had forgotten I loved, and arrived at sentences I would later type into my notebook. The mind, given time and no stimulus, does not become a blank. It becomes a garden. But because we weed it so constantly with images and pings, we never see what it would grow on its own. We are like farmers who cover the soil with concrete and then complain that nothing grows.

I don’t want to be a Luddite. I love the internet. I love that I can find the text of a medieval poem in seconds, or listen to a bird singing in another hemisphere, or video-call a friend in the mountains. But the medium’s bounty is also its poison. It offers so much that we lose the ability to appreciate any one thing. The whole world is in my pocket, and so the whole world is invisible. To make it visible again, I have to practice a kind of poverty. I have to decide, deliberately, to waste time. Not productively. Not “mindfully” as a wellness activity. Just to sit, and look, and let the mind idle. The engine of attention is not the accelerator. It is the clutch. It is the ability to disengage and to be still.

There is an ethical dimension to attention, too. To pay attention to another person is the most basic form of love. We say, “Be present,” but what we mean is: “For a moment, let your world become my world.” When you hold someone’s hand in a hospital room, you are not solving anything. You are not providing information or advice. You are simply witnessing. You are saying, with your body, “I am here, and I am not leaving, and this moment, with you, is enough.” That is what attention becomes when it is directed at a person. It is no longer a meditation or a technique. It is an act of courage.

I once sat with someone while they died. It was not a horror-show death, not a sudden accident, but a slow fading, after a long illness, with family around. The room was ordinary: pale blue walls, a laminated wooden crucifix, a plastic plant that no one had dusted in years. There was a window. The light came in low and gold, and I watched it travel across the floor. By the time the light reached the bed, the breath had stopped. That is the only way I can understand it. The light reached the bed. The breath stopped. There was no fanfare, no celestial choir. Just a small progress of light and the absence of a sound. I realized then that attention is the only thing we can leave with someone. The dead cannot receive our love anymore, except as memory. But the memory of being attended, of being watched with kindness, is not lost. It is stored in the attention itself, in the way we learn to hold the next person who is dying.

We are all, in one way or another, dying. Some of us are just earlier in the process. To pay attention is to say, “I know this, and I am not afraid.” It is to refuse the great lie of our age, which is that life is a problem to be solved, a series of obstacles to be overcome, a race to be won. Life is not a problem. It is a texture. It is a flavor. It is a field of light and shadow, and the only way to experience it is to notice it. That is why I write about dirty windows and tomato plants and the weight of a particular silence. Not because they are important, but because they are there. And because, if we do not notice them, we are not really here at all.

The light has moved. In the time it has taken me to write these pages, the sun has crossed the floor and climbed the opposite wall. The flyspecked window is now in shadow, and the kitchen is a duller place. But the dullness is not a loss. It is a change. Everything changes. The trick is to notice the changes without despairing of them.

I have written a kind of field guide, though it isn’t complete. A field guide should have entries for every species of the overlooked: the crack in the pavement, the smell of rain, the texture of a favorite shirt after it has been washed a hundred times, the sound of a distant train at night, the particular hum of the refrigerator that has become the percussion of silence. There are infinite entries. We will never finish the field guide, and that is exactly the point. The unfinishedness is the invitation. It is the door left open.

One last story. Last winter, I stood in my kitchen, waiting for water to boil. I was exhausted, not from anything dramatic, but from the cumulative weight of ordinary life. The phone was in my pocket. I did not take it out. Instead, I looked at the pot. The water at the bottom was utterly still, glassy, a tiny sheet of nothing. Then, after a minute, a single bubble appeared, clinging to the metal, quivering, growing, and finally releasing its small silver globe to rise. Another followed. Then a stream. Then the whole surface broke into motion. It was not a miracle. It was just water and heat and the laws of physics. But I watched it as if I had never seen water before, and in that moment, I had not. The previous water I had boiled was invisible, because I had been looking at my phone. This water was visible because I had chosen to notice. It tasted no different. The tea I made was the same tea. But the minute I spent watching the bubble was a minute that did not dissolve into the blur. It stayed. It stayed.

That is all I want to say. Pay attention. Not because you will be rewarded, not because it will make you a better person, not because it will save the planet. Pay attention because the water is boiling, because the light is moving, because the tomato is warm from the sun, because the person beside you is breathing. Pay attention because these are the only things that are real. The rest is noise. The rest is already gone.

Try this. Put down your phone and watch the light on the wall. Not the sun, not the window, not the clock. Just the light—the way it rests on the plaster, the slight trembling of its edge, the dust that hangs in its beam like a slow constellation. Do that for one minute. It will feel like an indulgence, then like an embarrassment, and finally, if you last long enough, like a revelation. The light moves. It moves? The earth moves, and the light is the messenger of that movement. It is the visible proof of spin, though we usually do not look long enough to see it.

I began to pay attention to such things by accident. I was waiting for something—a phone call, a test result, a letter that never arrived—and the waiting made ordinary surfaces unbearable and then unbearably interesting. The crack in the ceiling above my bed became a geography. The stain on the bookshelf became a Rorschach. The slow crawl of a spider across the baseboard became a narrative, complete with obstacles and a triumphant conclusion (the conclusion being that the spider disappeared into a crack and I did not see it die). This is what waiting does: it strips the world of its usefulness and leaves it as pure spectacle. It is the cheapest form of travel.

Attention is the only currency that cannot be inflated. There is always enough of it, yet we spend it as if it were worthless. We give it to screens that have been designed, by very intelligent people, to seize it and sell it. We give it to anxiety about the future and guilt about the past. We give it to the next thing before the present thing has even arrived. And then we wonder why time feels thin, why we cannot remember Tuesday, why the years slip by like water through a sieve. The paradox is that time does not slip by quickly; we slip by time quickly. To slow down, all we have to do is notice.

This is not a new idea. Every contemplative tradition says something like it. But I am not a mystic, and I don't intend to become one. I am just a person who has discovered that a dirty window, in the right light, can be as beautiful as a cathedral. There is a particular moment in late autumn, around four in the afternoon, when the sun comes through the west-facing window of my kitchen and strikes the flyspecked glass of the cabinet. The marks become a star chart. The pale yellow light reveals the film of grease left by years of cooking, the fingerprints of every meal I have ever made in that room. It is not clean, and that is the point. A spotless kitchen has no history. A clean window is just a hole. The dirty window is a text, written by time, illuminated by light.

I want to write a field guide to such texts. Not to grand landscapes, not to the Grand Canyon or the northern lights or the perfect beach at sunset—the postcard places where everyone already knows to look. I want to write about the overlooked. The architecture of a puddle. The voice of a radiator in December. The particular geometry of a grocery store parking lot at twilight. The way a plastic bag, caught in a bush, can look like a strange flower. The sound of your own breathing when you finally stop to listen to it. These are not escapes from the world. They are the world, if the world is large enough to include the insignificant.

Segment 2 (memory ~600 words):

When I was a child, my grandparents had a garden. It was not a beautiful garden. It was a working garden, a vegetable garden, full of weeds and stubborn soil and the skeletal remains of tomato cages. My grandfather would come in from it at dusk, his hands stained green, his shirt stuck to his back. He would set a basket of tomatoes on the counter and say, "Taste one." I did. It was warm from the sun, still dusty, and it tasted like nothing I have since encountered—not because tomatoes have changed, but because I have changed. The tomato was a verb. It was the entire August compressed into a single fragrant globe.

I could not have said that then. I would have said, "It's good," and run off to do something else. But the memory stayed, and it has become one of my most durable possessions. I carry it around like a coin in my pocket. Sometimes I take it out and examine it: the green smell of the vines, the white-painted farmhouse behind me, the sound of my grandmother singing along to a radio in a language I didn't understand. Why this moment and not a hundred others? I have asked myself this question for years. There is no answer. Memory is not a filing system. It is an ocean, and certain moments bob to the surface while others sink without a trace.

Proust had his madeleine. Marcel had his little cake, and I have my tasteless supermarket tomatoes, which are the exact opposite of the thing they recall. The madeleine is not a madeleine. It is any object that opens the door. For some people it is a song, a particular song from a particular summer, and for a second they are sixteen again, standing in a parking lot with the windows down. For others it is a smell: sunscreen, chlorine, rain on hot asphalt. These are not memories in the usual sense. They are resurrections. The past is not behind us. It is folded into the present, waiting for a cue.

We spend so much of our lives trying to escape the present—through memory, through anticipation, through the tiny anesthesia of the scroll—that we forget the present is the only place where the past can leak through. A friend of mine once said that nostalgia is not a longing for a time; it is a longing for a body. The body we had then. The knees that could kneel without pain, the eyes that did not need glasses, the skin that did not know the weight of years. The garden exists because my child-body existed in it. The tomato tastes the way it does because my mouth was new. Grief and wonder are the same organ, the sense that can touch the past.

And yet, I do not want to live in memory. The trick is to let memory dim the present just enough to give it depth, like a shadow in a painting. When I walk through the city today, I am walking through two cities: the one that is here and the one that used to be here. The drugstore where I bought my first concert ticket is now a laundromat. The movie theater has been torn down, and the parking lot has been filled with a sleek apartment building with a sign that says "LUXURY LIVING." The maple tree I used to climb is gone, but the shape of its absence is still visible in the skyline. A tree can die, but the negative space it leaves behind is a kind of monument.

The same is true for people. On the street I sometimes see a man who looks exactly like my father did when I was ten—same jacket, same way of holding his shoulders—and for a split second, hope surges: he is alive, he is young, he is walking toward me. Then the man turns, and it is not him, and the hope collapses into something like vertigo. But I do not want to stop having these moments. They are the proof that the past is not finished. They are the proof that love leaves an imprint, the way a body leaves a warm spot in a chair.

Segment 3 (art/writing ~500 words):

I am a writer, which means I spend a large part of my life failing to describe things. This is not a confession; it is a job description. The sunset cannot be captured. The face of a sleeping child cannot be captured. The exact weight of a particular silence, in a particular room, with a particular person, cannot be captured. And yet we keep trying. Why? Because the attempt to capture something is itself a way of paying attention. It is a way of asking the world to stay still long enough for us to love it.

Writing is an act of attention performed in public. A good description is not a photograph; it is a map. The map, as every cartographer knows, is not the territory. But a good map can teach you to see the territory for yourself. It can point to a hill and say, "Look, there is a hill," and when you look, you see the hill, and you also see something the map did not include—a bird, a shadow, a wind that moves the grass. The map's grammar is not the world's grammar, but it can rhyme with it.

I have a notebook full of failed descriptions. It is my favorite possession. I open it and read: "The fog came in like a cat that does not want to be petted." That is a good simile, but it is also a lie. The fog has no intention. It is only fog. The simile is a map of my feeling, not of the fog. Another entry: "The station clock is permanently ten minutes fast, and the green light above the platform buzzes like a trapped fly." This is almost a description, but it omits the most important thing: the smell of diesel and rain, the sound of a woman's heels receding on the platform, the fact that I was late and did not care. Too much to include. The writer must choose, and every choice is a loss.

But sometimes, rarely, a description fails so beautifully that it creates a new organ of perception. I read a poem about a river and, for a week, I cannot look at a river without hearing the poet's sound. I read a novel about a city and, for a month, the city is thicker. The novel has added a ghost floor to every building, a secret passage to every street. This is not magic. It is simply the power of one person's attention, transmitted through black marks on a page, to teach another person how to look. It is the same power that makes a parent say to a child, "See the moon?" and the child, looking up, sees the moon for the first time even though it has been there every night. We do not see the world. We see what we have been taught to see. Attention is learned. Wonder is a skill.

Segment 4 (digital distraction ~500 words):

Of course, attention is a contested territory. I do not need to describe the screen; you are reading this on one. It is the world's most effective attention trap, and I am using it while denouncing it. That is the peculiar position of anyone who writes about distraction: you cannot escape the medium you address. But I can at least tell the truth about my own experience. When I am scrolling, I am not paying attention. I am being taken for a ride. My eyes move across a river of opinions, advertisements, photographs, outrage, all of it engineered to produce a micro-response—a jab of anger, a pinch of envy, a brief, hollow amusement. Each response resets the clock. The algorithm dangles the next bait. It is as if someone had invented a machine for the express purpose of converting my life into a series of ten-second glances, and then paid me no wages.

The strange thing is that I know this. We all know this. And yet the compulsion persists. The phone is not a tool; it is a companion, a pet, an appendage. I have caught myself stroking its screen as if it were a cat. I have reached for it in the middle of a conversation with a friend, and then realized what I was doing, and then realized that I was reaching for it again to escape the shame of having reached for it. The only way out is not through willpower, which is finite and easily exhausted. It is through the reclamation of boredom. We have forgotten how to be bored. We treat boredom as an emergency, as a symptom to be suppressed. But boredom is the antechamber of attention. It is the empty room where wonder can enter.

Some of my most profound experiences have occurred while doing apparently nothing. Waiting for bread to rise. Staring out the window of a train. Lying in bed and watching the shadows of leaves move on the ceiling. In these moments, I have solved problems I did not know I had, remembered people I had forgotten I loved, and arrived at sentences I would later type into my notebook. The mind, given time and no stimulus, does not become a blank. It becomes a garden. But because we weed it so constantly with images and pings, we never see what it would grow on its own. We are like farmers who cover the soil with concrete and then complain that nothing grows.

I don't want to be a Luddite. I love the internet. I love that I can find the text of a medieval poem in seconds, or listen to a bird singing in another hemisphere, or video-call my friend in the mountains. But the medium's bounty is also its poison. It offers so much that we lose the ability to appreciate any one thing. The whole world is in my pocket, and so the whole world is invisible. To make it visible again, I have to practice a kind of poverty. I have to decide, deliberately, to waste time. Not productively. Not "mindfully" as a wellness activity. Just to sit, and look, and let the mind idle. The engine of attention is not the accelerator. It is the clutch. It is the ability to disengage and to be still.

Segment 5 (ethics and love ~400 words):

There is an ethical dimension to attention, too. To pay attention to another person is the most basic form of love. We say, "Be present," but what we mean is: "For a moment, let your world become my world." When you hold someone's hand in a hospital room, you are not solving anything. You are not providing information or advice. You are simply witnessing. You are saying, with your body, "I am here, and I am not leaving, and this moment, with you, is enough." That is what attention becomes when it is directed at a person. It is no longer a meditation or a technique. It is an act of courage.

I once sat with someone while they died. It was not a horror-show death, not a sudden accident, but a slow-fading, after a long illness, with family around. The room was ordinary: pale blue walls, a laminated wooden crucifix, a plastic plant that no one had dusted in years. There was a window. The light came in low and gold, and I watched it travel across the floor. By the time the light reached the bed, the breath had stopped. That is the only way I can understand it. The light reached the bed. The breath stopped. There was no fanfare, no celestial choir. Just a small progress of light and the absence of a sound. I realized then that attention is the only thing we can leave with someone. The dead cannot receive our love anymore, except as memory. But the memory of being attended, of being watched with kindness, is not lost. It is stored in the attention itself, in the way we learn to hold the next person who is dying.

We are all, in one way or another, dying. Some of us are just earlier in the process. To pay attention is to say, "I know this, and I am not afraid." It is to refuse the great lie of our age, which is that life is a problem to be solved, a series of obstacles to be overcome, a race to be won. Life is not a problem. It is a texture. It is a flavor. It is a field of light and shadow, and the only way to experience it is to notice it. That is why I write about dirty windows and tomato plants and the weight of a particular silence. Not because they are important, but because they are there. And because, if we do not notice them, we are not really here at all.

Segment 6 (return / closing ~400 words):

The light has moved. In the time it has taken me to write these pages, the sun has crossed the floor and climbed the opposite wall. The flyspecked window is now in shadow, and the kitchen is a duller place. But the dullness is not a loss. It is a change. Everything changes. The trick is to notice the changes without despairing of them.

I have written a kind of field guide, though it isn't complete. A field guide should have entries for every species of the overlooked: the crack in the pavement, the smell of rain, the texture of a favorite shirt after it has been washed a hundred times, the sound of a distant train at night, the particular hum of the refrigerator that has become the percussion of silence. There are infinite entries. We will never finish the field guide, and that is exactly the point. The unfinishedness is the invitation. It is the door left open.

One last story. Last winter, I stood in my kitchen, waiting for water to boil. I was exhausted, not from anything dramatic, but from the cumulative weight of ordinary life. The phone was in my pocket. I did not take it out. Instead, I looked at the pot. The water at the bottom was utterly still, glassy, a tiny sheet of nothing. Then, after a minute, a single bubble appeared, clinging to the metal, quivering, growing, and finally releasing its small silver globe to rise. Another followed. Then a stream. Then the whole surface broke into motion. It was not a miracle. It was just water and heat and the laws of physics. But I watched it as if I had never seen water before, and in that moment, I had not. The previous water I had boiled was invisible, because I had been looking at my phone. This water was visible because I had chosen to notice. It tasted no different. The tea I made was the same tea. But the minute I spent watching the bubble was a minute that did not dissolve into the blur. It stayed. It stayed.

That is all I want to say. Pay attention. Not because you will be rewarded, not because it will make you a better person, not because it will save the planet. Pay attention because the water is boiling, because the light is moving, because the tomato is warm from the sun, because the person beside you is breathing. Pay attention because these are the only things that are real. The rest is noise. The rest is already gone.
